There are deloads, where you reduce intensity for a while (e.g., 60% for a week) and then return to your previous levels. This is useful to allow for more complete recovery without losing progress.

Then there are resets, where you decrease your working weight (e.g., -10%) and start progressing again from that point. This is helpful for overcoming plateaus.

You're attempting to use a reset when you would typically use a deload. If you need a deload week, take one. Similarly, if you want to use smaller increments, do that. Or if you've exhausted all you can from a linear progression, switch to a different approach.

However, one of the best ways to hinder your progress is to intentionally avoid it. Don't reset just because it's challenging; it's meant to be challenging.

Put a bar on your back, and step on a scale. Note the reading. Now pull on the bar as hard as you like. See if the scale reading changes.

Technically yes, the hands are exerting a downward force *on the bar*. But we don't care about the bar, we care about the combined bar-and-lifter system. By Newton's Third Law, the bar is exerting an exactly equal upward force on your hands, so the net force on the bar-lifter system is zero. Simultaneously, there is a normal (contact) force from your back onto the bar, which prevents the bar from accelerating downward as your hands pull on it. The contact force from the bar onto your back prevents you from being accelerated upwards as the bar pulls on your hands. These forces again cancel out for a net force of zero on the system.

It's the same reason you can't levitate by pulling on your own bootstraps. Forces internal to a system never generate net force on the system, because this would violate Newton's Third Law and also the conservation of momentum.

You're confused because you have the wrong idea of what bulking and cutting do.

You should lose little or no strength while cutting; frequently you will even gain strength, just more slowly. If you track your performance metrics, you should find that they increase due to your dropping bodyweight, even if your lifts regress a little. If your performance metrics are decreasing, you're cutting wrong.

The other thing is that you should be spending WAY less than half of your time cutting. In a year, you don't spend 6 months bulking and 6 months cutting. You can cut fat faster than you can build muscle, and only some of the weight you gain while bulking needs to be cut, since you obviously don't want to cut away the muscle mass you've gained. If you bulk for 10 months (gaining 20 pounds), you can cut for 2 months (losing 10 pounds) and be right back at your starting level of body fat, except with +10 pounds of muscle.

So you can have 10 months of training with the full benefit of a calorie surplus (plus maybe some progress during your cut) if you bulk and cut, or 12 months at maintenance if you don't. Eating a lot is *really really important* for adding strength and size, so bulking is usually the better plan.

This is a broad topic that you probably aren't going to really understand from reading a general encyclopedia page and an online comment. But here's something that might help a bit.

First, let's talk about real numbers. The real numbers are sort of an 'expansion' of the rational numbers. Specifically, we start with the rational numbers in the usual way, imagining them arranged on a number line. The rationals are dense on this line, but the line still has holes in it: for example, there's no square root of 2. We have rationals that square to something really close to 2; in fact, we can get arbitrarily close. But we can't get there exactly. This means the rationals are *incomplete*: you can write down a sequence of rationals that looks like it ought to have a limit of sqrt(2), except there isn't any such number.

To build the reals, we "fill in" all of these holes. The machinery we use to do this is technical and I'm going to skip over it completely. Suffice to say, this process takes all those sequences that look like they *ought* to converge, and makes new numbers for them to converge towards. These irrationals are what you would expect them to look like as the limits of rational approximations. The sequence I mentioned above might look like (1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, ...) and sure enough the square root of 2 looks like 1.414...

Now the p-adics are built by *exactly* the same process - except we change what it means for a sequence to converge. We no longer care about size in the usual sense. Instead, we're going to care about *congruence*. But for that we need to pick a modulus, and for technical reasons it has to be a prime number.

For example, let's take p=3. We're going to start from scratch again, with the rational numbers, except instead of talking about the usual distance, we're going to talk about congruence mod 3. Numbers that are congruent are close together. Specifically, we're going to say that the distance between them is the *reciprocal* of the highest power of 3 by which they are congruent. (The *p-adic absolute value* generalizes the idea of congruence-as-distance to all rational numbers.)

So 0 is close to 3, they're a distance of 1/3 apart. And 0 is even closer to 9, they're a distance of 1/9 apart. But 0 is not close to 1, so they're a distance of 1 unit apart. Similarly, 1 is close to 4, even closer to 10, and not close to 2.

Think about it for a second, and you'll see that every integer must be close (ie, congruent mod 3) to either 0, 1, or 2. So we can take all of our integers and put them into 3 groups around those numbers. Within each group, we can subdivide again: the integers congruent to 0 mod 3 are either of the form 3n, 3n+3, or 3n+6 - so we have three smaller groups, representing congruence mod 9. Subdivide again into groups mod 27. And so on. Instead of a number line, you have arranged your integers into a picture that looks like a fractal structure.

But just like the number line, this picture has holes in it. I can get things that are close to square roots of -2! Look:

* 2^(2)=4, which is congruent to -2 mod 3.
* 4^(2)=16, which is congruent to -2 mod 3^(2).
* 22^(2)=484, which is congruent to -2 mod 3^(3) (actually, mod 3^(5)).

In fact, I can extend this sequence as far as I want, and get a rational number that squares to something arbitrarily close to -2 (in our 3-adic congruence sense). The fact I can get arbitrarily close is a result from number theory, which I'm not going to prove here.

So under our congruence scheme, it looks like we have a hole where there should be a sqrt(-2). We can fill in those holes, just like we did before. Instead of the reals, we get the 3-adic numbers, and sure enough there is a 3-adic square root of -2.

What does it look like? Well, it turns out that the most convenient way to write numbers for 3-adic math is in base 3. Then my approximations above would be written (2, 12, 212, ...). And as you'd expect, the exact 3-adic square root of -2 looks like ...212.

In the reals, digits are allowed to go infinitely out to the *right* because huge negative powers of 10 are considered "small". But in the 3-adics, digits are allowed to go infinitely far to the *left*, because huge *positive* powers of 3 are considered "small".

A transformation matrix is what you use when you want to change into a different basis, perform a transformation in that basis, and then change back to your original basis.

Here, we're not changing basis at all. We're just applying the transformation directly: rotating around an axis, represented by multiplying on the left. A rotation around the z-axis gives a vector obtained from rotating a given vector around the z-axis.
